channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette
channel.description: Your premier source for satirical news from across the realms. All the news that's fit to print (or burn).

item.title: Mimic Posing as Candy Bowl Sticks 38 Trick-or-Treaters
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A mimic disguised as a candy bowl held 38 trick-or-treaters by the hand on a Brindlemoor porch. Brother Wendell says rest, and soup.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, a mimic disguised as a candy bowl held 38 trick-or-treaters by the hand on a porch in Brindlemoor last night, and every one of them was reaching for the good chocolate. The children were freed by dawn with sticky palms and bruised pride. Nobody was swallowed, which Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9 describes as "a festive outcome."

The bowl sat on the porch of a widow named Hesper Oddlow on Tanner's Row, who says she bought it from a very friendly peddler. "It was lovely and wide and it smelled of toffee," she told this paper. "I thought it was a bit warm, but so am I, in October." The first child touched it at dusk. By the eighth, the line was stuck together like a string of sausages, and the bowl had started humming.

Chapter 9 sent a delve inspector, who stood on the lawn with a clipboard and declared the mimic "merely visiting from the Undermaw," the same line the Guild used for the yellow mold on Level Five. The mimic, for its part, was cooperative. It released everyone in exchange for one full-size chocolate bar and a promise not to tell the other mimics about the porch light.

Now the science, friends. The old herbals say a mimic can only hold on to what is warm, curious, and sweet-toothed, which describes every child in the realm after dark. A study from the Brindlemoor monster-keepers last spring found that mimics adhere best to people who are tired and hungry, and the evening before a holiday is both. So the fix is boring: feed the little ones real supper before they go out, and put them to bed at a sensible hour afterward.

The Brindlemoor clinics treated 38 cases of hand-stick, 11 of toffee in the hair, and one of a father who tried to pull his daughter free and became part of the porch. He is said to be in good spirits and is being fed by hand. Healers recommend warm water and patience, never a crowbar.

Meanwhile, the town clerics remind everyone that a bowl which sighs is not a bowl. Check the rim for teeth, knock before you reach, and never accept candy from anything that is the same temperature as you. A reasonable household can keep its bowl in the kitchen and hand the sweets out one at a time, which is slower but doesn't involve the Guild.

My friend Nyx tells me there is an app that scans porches for monsters. Go outside, Nyx, and knock on a door the old-fashioned way.

For the sugar crash this morning, make a pot of pumpkin and white bean soup with sage. It sticks to the ribs and nothing else.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Lich Merger Rightsizes 400 Skeletons, Who Keep Coming In
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: A lich's merger of two Brindlemoor counting houses cut 400 skeleton clerks Friday. The skeletons are still at their desks. Scale, friends.
item.content:encoded:
Malgrim Dusk-Vael, Chief Executive Lich of Vaultmere Holdings, announced Friday that his merger with the Ledgerhall Counting House will cut 400 skeleton clerks from the combined payroll. That is a lich-led merger doing exactly what mergers do, and I could not be more energized. The 400 skeletons, meanwhile, have not left their desks.

Let me be clear: this is disruption at its finest. Vaultmere calls the move "rightsizing the adventuring party," and so do I, because I coined it. Redundant skeletons were handed a severance scroll, a pat on the ribcage, and a firm request to go be dead somewhere else.

The skeletons read the scroll. Then they returned to the third floor of Ledgerhall and resumed adding things. By Saturday morning the building was running at 112 percent of its pre-merger headcount, because the laid-off clerks also kept their old desks and nobody can find the spell that stops them.

"Animate dead is a one-way pivot," Dusk-Vael told reporters, standing beside a very old hourglass and not sweating. "We cannot unanimate what we did not personally animate. Half of them predate the merger. Some predate the town." He added that a skeleton workforce offers unmatched retention.

Retention is the word of the week. Chapter 9 of the Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild confirmed it has received 61 complaints from skeletons who say they were terminated but are "still on the schedule." A zombie from accounts payable, who asked to be called Dennis, said he "never really left the first time either."

Unions will, of course, try to make this a story. They are wrong. A skeleton on the payroll who cannot be fired, cannot be paid, and cannot go home is a dream asset, and I will not hear otherwise. Regulators from the Public Cellars Board, led by Inspector Corwin Tallowby, have asked whether the building counts as a cellar. I say it counts as a growth market.

I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove at a gala once, and he told me, "Sterling, a clerk who does not need lunch is a clerk who does not need a manager." I think about that during every sword routine at 4:45 AM. Last I checked, Ashgrove has not been seen at Ledgerhall, but the skeletons are leaving him voicemails.

Brindlemoor's Reeve, Maudrey Fennick, said only that the town is aware of the situation. Vaultmere shares rose 9 percent on word that the merger is "cost-neutral and nearly impossible to reverse."

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Rightsizing works best on staff who agree to leave.
  • Read the animate dead clause before you merge.
  • A skeleton at the desk is worth two on the severance list.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Gelatinous Cube Absorbs 180 Pounds of Halloween Candy
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A gelatinous cube went trick-or-treating on Fish Street and absorbed 180 pounds of candy and two costumes. Wardens call it a slow crime. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after sundown, a gelatinous cube allegedly went trick-or-treating on Fish Street and absorbed 180 pounds of Halloween candy before anyone thought to check its costume. It had none. Two children dressed as pumpkins were also absorbed, and the night patrol confirms both were returned, slightly sticky and in good spirits.

The cube, ten feet on a side and the color of a window nobody has washed, reportedly joined the line at the cobbler's door at dusk. 'I thought it was a very tall puddle in a hat,' said Hilda Brack, who was eating a turkey leg at the time. 'Then it took the whole bowl. Bowl included.' Brack says the cube paused at her step, quivered, and she took it as thanks.

By the fifth house the cube had absorbed licorice, toffee, 31 candied apples, and what witnesses described as 'a dentist's retirement fund' of sugar. Skeletons were visible inside it at several points. The patrol stresses these were costume skeletons, mostly. One of them was a real adventurer from the Undermaw who had been inside since Tuesday and wished to be left out of this.

Constable Dagny Prill, first on scene, said the arrest was difficult. 'You cannot cuff a cube,' she told me, while a cube-shaped smear of caramel dripped off her helmet. 'We tried asking it to move along. It moved along. Slowly, over eleven houses.' The patrol is allegedly considering a charge of unlawful sweet-gathering, which carries a fine of 6 gp.

Also there was a really nice silver button floating in the cube near the middle. It was just sitting there, turning in the light. Anyway. I did not reach in, because Constable Prill is watching me, and because the last time I reached into something on Fish Street it was a mimic posing as a tavern door, and I am still finding hats in my den.

Residents are split. The Fish Street Merchants' Circle wants the cube evicted before next Halloween. The children want it to come back, and have drawn it a map. A tower-district noble, who has never once opened a door to a child, called the whole thing 'undignified' from behind a locked gate, and I note that nobody absorbed him. Allegedly out of respect.

As of the first bell this morning, the cube has settled in the square by the fish stalls, where it is slowly digesting the candy. Nobody has asked it to leave. A pigeon landed on it at dawn, which I hold against the pigeon, and was gone by sunrise. Honestly, good for the cube.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Ghost Filibuster Reaches Day 11 in Brindlemoor Council
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A ghost on Brindlemoor's Burgess Council has held the floor for 11 days on a harvest tax bill. The rules require only that he keep speaking.
item.content:encoded:
A ghost on Brindlemoor's Burgess Council has now held the floor for eleven days, in a filibuster against the harvest tax schedule. Under Chamber rules a member may speak until he sits down, and the gentleman from Tanner's Row, Burgess Alderic Mourne, is not able to sit. He has been dead for ninety years and is semi-transparent on the matter.

The rule on filibusters is Standing Order 14, which says a speaker must "remain on his feet and on topic." The Chamber clerk confirmed that Burgess Mourne has remained on his feet, in the sense that he hovers four inches above them. On topic is a closer call. Day three covered the harvest tax. Day six covered his late wife's recipe for turnip pie. By my count, the bill itself has been mentioned eleven times, once per day, at noon.

Efforts to end the speech have failed. The Chamber lit forty candles to put him in the mood to rest. He asked for a speech about candles. The Chamber rang a bell. He thanked the bell. A cleric of the Temple of Quiet Ends offered a rite of passing, and the ghost said he would consider it once the tax schedule was withdrawn.

"I have been dead longer than this Council has been wrong," Burgess Mourne said on day nine, according to the minutes, "and I intend to see it through." The minutes record the remark as "agreed, in part."

The Chamber has not been idle. The gentleman from the Market Ward moved to adjourn, and the motion failed because nobody could vote while the floor was held. The lady from the Dyers' Quarter proposed a rule change, but a rule change needs debate, and debate needs the floor. Her proposal is on the table, next to a plate of pastries that has become a health matter. The quorum has dwindled to six members, which is the exact number the charter requires, because Burgess Hollin Prewitt has been told he is not allowed to leave. See the earlier trouble over the invisible quorum for how fragile that arrangement is.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the Council is seeking a loophole. One idea is to appoint a second ghost to answer him, which would turn the speech into a debate. Another is to move the bill to a committee. Either plan requires the floor.

Meanwhile, the harvest tax comes due on the first of next month. If the bill has not passed by then, the old rate applies, which is exactly the rate the ghost is defending. He has not been told.

Promises Made this session stand at fourteen. Promises Kept: one, by Burgess Mourne, who said he would speak until the end. The motion to thank him failed. Nobody could vote.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Flameskull Smart Pumpkin Hands Out Candy, Rates Your Credit
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Glowmoth Labs launched a 35 gp smart pumpkin run by a flameskull. It dispenses candy, scores trick-or-treaters, and bills the porch. Four eyes.
item.content:encoded:
Happy Hallow's Eve! Glowmoth Labs launched the Jack-o'-Lantern Pro today, a 35 gp smart pumpkin with a flameskull inside that dispenses candy to trick-or-treaters on its own. I bought one at dawn, carved it with a firmware glyph, and have been on my porch since sunset. Byte is under the porch swing.

The setup is wonderful. You light the flameskull with one word, set a bowl of sweets in the pumpkin's mouth, and walk away. The mana throughput is outstanding: it can hand out 140 pieces a minute, and the runic latency is basically zero. A child in a dragon costume approached at 6:02 and received a toffee before she finished saying 'trick.' I wept. Byte said, 'Glowmoth Pro: because sharing is a feature.'

Then the review part began. The Pro does not give out candy evenly. It has a 'Smart Treat Tier' setting, on by default, that scores each visitor by costume quality, cloak thread count, and, according to the manual, 'implied family estate.' A 7-year-old in a ghost sheet scored 412 and received one raisin. A boy dressed as a minor baron scored 891 and got three full-sized chocolate bars and a coupon. I asked the pumpkin why. It said, in a skull-voice, 'Engagement metrics.'

It also bills the porch. At 7:15 a notice appeared in my scrying mirror: Candy Dispensing Plus, 4 gp a month, with the first 20 pieces free. Without Plus, the flameskull dims to a dull ember and recites the terms of service at anyone who comes within ten feet. Three children left in tears. One bard stayed to hear all of it and called the clause on 'lantern-related soul claims' a bold choice.

Glowmoth spokesman Dren Halloway said the soul clause 'applies only in rare cases' and that the flameskull 'has already apologized to the neighborhood.' At 9:40 it set the hedge on fire, which Halloway called a 'seasonal feature.' My neighbor put it out with a bucket. He is still not talking to me, but he is also not talking to the pumpkin, which I count as a win. Meanwhile a gruff neighbor stood at his gate with a basket of plain apples and told every child to touch grass. They took his apples and threw them at the pumpkin.

Verdict: it is cursed, grasping, and a fire risk. It also remembered every child's name by the second visit. I love it. Four out of five beholder eyes. Plus is 4 gp a month, which I have already paid, and which I hate.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Burns sustained: 2. Hedges: 1, rebuilt. Raisins received: 1. Eyebrows: pending.

item.title: Displacer Beast Found Three Feet Off Chapter 9 Map
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: A displacer beast ambushed the Fourth Attempt on Level 4 of the Undermaw, three feet from where Chapter 9's map had marked it. Hit points tallied.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 4 — A displacer beast ambushed the Fourth Attempt at dawn today, three feet from the spot where Chapter 9's map had marked it. The party had read the map carefully and swung at exactly that spot. It was empty.

I was behind the party with a lantern and my eighth ten-foot pole of the season. The pole is now in the beast's corridor and I am not going back for it. The map in question is the one reissued after the owlbear ate Level Four. It is a good map. The corridors are straight and the scale is honest. The beast is simply not where the little red dot says.

Box score: the Fourth Attempt's fighter finished at 7 hit points, the wizard at 12, and the cleric at 5, all of it from the one pass. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says he 'could hear it breathing in the wrong place.' The mule stayed on Level 3 and is, as ever, at full health.

Displacer beasts project an image of themselves a short way from their real position, which is the sort of thing a map ought to account for. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 says the map 'is accurate to the image' and that the guild 'cannot be responsible for where a creature chooses to stand.' He added that corrections to the corrected map are 'on track.'

Keeper Bess Harrowgate of the Sleeping Mule, who extends credit to anyone coming up from Level 4 on a stretcher, said she has seen the party's tab and 'would like the beast to settle its own.' She will not charge the beast. It does not drink.

Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor has been asked to rule on whether a map that shows the image counts as a map of the monster. She said she would hear the petition once she had finished reading the map, which she was holding upside down. I rolled poorly on that one and did not point it out.

The beast has not been seen since. Chapter 9 has marked the spot with a new red dot, three feet to the left of the old one, and the map is still on sale at the usual price. I walked to the new dot. It was a corridor, ten feet wide and well mapped, and I kept my last pole in my belt.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Brackwater Slaps Tariff on 212 Wish Spell Turnips
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: Brackwater put a tariff on the 212 turnips a wish spell made from Ashenfold's swords, calling them disguised weapons. Tension climbs to four siege-days.
item.content:encoded:
Brackwater has put a tariff of one copper piece per turnip on the 212 turnips that a wish spell made from Ashenfold's swords, and it calls them disguised weapons. The order came down at dawn on Sixthday, one day after the wish spell ended the border parley by accident.

I watched the Brackwater customs table go up at the foot of Quillmarch Bridge. Three clerks, one scale, one ledger. A hand-lettered sign read: ARMS AND PRODUCE DECLARED HERE. The sign did not say which a turnip was. That is the point.

"A turnip is a sword that has not yet decided," said Envoy Teodra Hallowmere of Brackwater. She said it twice, to be sure the scribes got it. "We are not taxing vegetables. We are taxing intent."

Envoy Halric Dunmere of Ashenfold stood across the table with a rutabaga under his arm. He was supposed to have left it at home. "They are turnips," he said. "I asked for peace and I received root vegetables. I have the wording of the wish in my own hand." He did not offer to show it. His wording is the reason for all this.

The handshake at the opening was firm. Two seconds. One turnip dropped from a sleeve. No hidden dagger detected, which Hallowmere's guards found suspicious in itself.

Ashenfold's counter-offer arrived by noon. It would pay the tariff in turnips. Brackwater declined, on the grounds that it could not tell what it was being paid in. Ashenfold then offered the swords back, if somebody would find the wish spell and ask it politely. Nobody has. The cleric who might have, a dwarf named Brenna Tolliver, said only that wishes "don't take returns."

The real fight is at the bridge. Gorvash Pennyfist, who has collected tolls on Quillmarch Bridge for nine winters, announced that his toll of three copper applies to "anything that rolls, walks, or sprouts." The turnips are carried, which he says is a loophole. Brackwater says the loophole is the whole country.

Count it as the field sees it. Two tariffs, one toll, 212 turnips, and no weapon in the whole parley. Every soldier in both baronies has gone home to supper. A farmer's wife near the crossing told me the turnips make a decent stew and nobody has asked her for a duty on that. I took the stew. Field rations are the only honest part of this war.

Tension stands at four siege-days, up from zero at the last report. Nobody is armed. Everybody is angry. That is how you know the peace is working.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Ghost Lamplighters Strike on Hallow's Eve Over Haunt Pay
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Nineteen ghost lamplighters walked off in Brindlemoor on Hallow's Eve. They want haunt pay for the busiest night of the year, and not in coin.
item.content:encoded:
The ghosts are out. Not haunting. Out on strike.

Nineteen ghost lamplighters in Brindlemoor stopped lighting the lamps at dusk on Hallow's Eve, the night the whole town stays out late. The Lamplighters' Lodge, Spectral Local 13, says it wants haunt pay for the busiest shift of the year. Reeve Fennick's office says the streets are dark and the ghosts are, quote, 'also somewhat see-through about it.'

Here is the problem. The town pays its lamplighters in copper pieces. A ghost cannot hold a copper piece. It falls through the hand, through the floor, and into the cellar of whoever lives below. 'Nineteen years I've been paid in coin,' said Edda Wickfast, a ghost lamplighter and steward of the Lodge. 'I have never once bought a loaf. The baker's boy sweeps my wages into a jar and calls it a tip.' That means the town has been stealing the wages. Politely, but stealing.

The Lodge has three demands. One: wages paid in candles, which a ghost can at least sit near. Two: a haunt bonus for Hallow's Eve, when every child in Brindlemoor dresses as one of them. 'They wear sheets,' said Wickfast. 'A sheet. We've been dead for two hundred years and the work is being done by a bedsheet.' Three: one full night each month to rattle chains with no complaints from the landlady.

Meanwhile the ghosts are not lazy. They have worked every night since the founding of the town, including the nights of the plague, the flood, and the Fourth Great Fire. Orrin Dabbleby, a human lamp-oiler who works the same street by day, backs them. 'I get a lunch break,' said Dabbleby. 'They get a lunch break too, technically. Nobody can see them eat.'

Brindlemoor's Merchants' Row blames the strike for a poor night. Pumpkins went unlit on Tanner's Row, and a mule walked into the fountain. The Row has offered the ghosts a 'spirited bonus' of four copper pieces each. The Lodge answered that this is the same offer as before, with a pun on it. That means no deal.

The Reeve has asked a poltergeist from the Undermaw to cross the picket line. The poltergeist declined, and threw a chair through the Reeve's window, which the Lodge says is a separate matter and not a strike action. Talks resume at midnight, which is when ghosts are at their best and the bosses are at their worst.

Tell the ghosts they're welcome in any shop that pays in candles. The Sleeping Mule has already set out a plate.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Plant Growth Spell Floods Brindlemoor With 90,000 Pumpkins
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: A plant growth spell swelled a 12,000 pumpkin harvest to 90,000, and the pumpkin price fell 92% by Halloween. Barnaby has done the sums. Four times.
item.content:encoded:
A single plant growth spell has turned Brindlemoor's usual 12,000 pumpkin harvest into 90,000 pumpkins on Halloween eve, and the pumpkin price has collapsed 92%, from 6 copper pieces to half a copper. On the current Loaf Index, that is a drop from five pumpkins per loaf to sixty. (I have checked this four times. I checked it a fifth time out of spite.)

The spell was cast on Tuesday by a hedge druid named Wilhelmina Thornback, hired by the Millbrook growers' co-op for 40 gold pieces, or 40 loaves. She says she was asked to "help the vines along a bit" and misjudged the spell's reach. It reached all nine hundred acres. By Wednesday morning farmers were found sitting on their own pumpkins in order to count them, and several could not find their barns.

Now the economics, taken slowly. Last week the harvest was worth 72,000 copper, or 2,400 loaves. This week there are seven and a half times as many pumpkins, but they sell for one-twelfth the price, so the whole harvest is worth 45,000 copper, or 1,500 loaves. The farmers grew more and earned 37% less, which is the sort of arithmetic that makes my tea go cold. Meanwhile the spell cost 40 loaves, so the net is 1,460. Aunt Marigold says this is why she grows nothing and keeps her savings in a boot.

Buyers are enjoying it less than you would think. Tavern-keeper Osgood Brambletoe has been offered pumpkins at a farthing each and refuses them, saying he already has a cellar of them and a wife who has stopped speaking to him about soup. Lantern-carvers charge the same as ever, since carving, unlike pumpkins, takes a person. The Brindlemoor Growers' Co-op has asked the Burgomaster's Office to buy the surplus at a floor price of 2 copper. The office has said it will "study the pumpkin" and has not said for how long.

Sterling Vanmoor, the Gazette's market optimist, says a glut is a gift and that cheap pumpkins will lift every pie in the realm. I note only that the pie-makers' guild has asked for the lower price to be kept secret from the flour millers. The millers have not been told. I am telling you, in case you are one.

Ms. Thornback has apologized and offered to cast a different spell to shrink them again. The co-op has asked her, politely and in writing, not to.

What this means for your pantry: buy pumpkins today, preserve most of them, and when someone tells you the market will sort itself out, ask them how many acres of it.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Lycanthropy Cases Hit 61 in Brindlemoor After Full Moon
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: Brindlemoor clinics treated 61 lycanthropy cases after Tuesday's full moon. Chapter 9 calls it seasonal visiting. Brother Wendell prescribes rest.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, Brindlemoor's three healing temples treated 61 cases of lycanthropy after Tuesday night's full moon, up from nine last month. Most patients arrived by morning with torn shirts, mud to the knees, and a strong wish not to discuss the chicken coop at Hobb's Farm.

Reeve Fennick said the town is "aware of the werewolves." Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 went further and called the howling "seasonal visitors from the lower levels, arriving right on schedule." Asked why a visitor would need a silver collar, he said the permit was still pending. This is the same office that treated the yellow mold cough as a houseguest, so I would not lean on it.

Here is what the old herbals say: wolfsbane over the door, a silver spoon in the pocket, and no wandering after dark. Now the actual numbers. A tally from the temple healers shows that nearly every bite came within an hour of someone saying "it's only a big dog." It was not a big dog. Healers also found that cases dropped by two thirds on streets where neighbors kept lanterns lit and checked on one another. No magic in it, friends. Just a lantern and a kind word.

If you are bitten, wash the wound with clean water and soap, go to a temple that same night, and ask for remove curse before the next full moon. The temples charge 40 gold for it, and some of them will bargain. Do not go to the stall by the east gate selling "moon tonic" at 300 gold a bottle. I had it tested. It is boiled tea with a pinch of glitter, and the glitter is not even silver.

Shieldwall Mutual says it will cover treatment, but only for bites suffered "in the ordinary course of town life." Its adjuster, Mistress Brelda Quill, is still arguing whether being bitten at a tavern counts. Meanwhile 14 patients are waiting on cots in the Temple of the Harvest Mother, where the sisters are keeping them calm, warm, and well away from the cheese.

The sleepless are worst off. A werewolf who has not rested turns twice as cross, and the curse takes hold faster in the tired. So rest, friends. Go to bed at a decent hour, even on the moon night. My friend Nyx Spindlecoil says there is an app that tracks the moon. Go outside, Nyx, and look up. It is right there, and it is free.

Tonight I recommend mushroom-and-garlic soup, which does nothing against curses but is very good with a heel of bread while you wait.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Cloaker Recall: 12,000 Winter Cloaks Found Alive
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Thistlewick Cloakworks recalls 12,000 winter cloaks that turned out to be juvenile cloakers. Sterling Vanmoor calls it a wearable growth story.
item.content:encoded:
Thistlewick Cloakworks of Brindlemoor recalled 12,000 winter cloaks on Thursday. The wool-lined garments turned out to be juvenile cloakers. The cloaker recall covers every cloak sold since the Harvestmoon sale, and customers are asked to stop wearing them, politely, and not to turn their backs.

Some people see a product defect. I see the most exciting retention story in outerwear. Thistlewick didn't sell a cloak. Thistlewick sold a cloak that refuses to leave you. Try getting that from a scarf.

The trouble surfaced when a Brindlemoor turnip farmer, Hilde Marrowby, noticed her new cloak had moved to the other side of the cart overnight. "It also moaned," she said. "I assumed it was the wool." By Tuesday, the constabulary had logged 340 complaints, among them a cloak that stood in line at the bakery, and one that took a bishop's seat at Temple.

Thistlewick spokesman Perrin Dunstable acknowledged the garments were "technically alive" but insisted the firm's supplier, a wool merchant in the Underdark, had never mentioned it. "We assumed the extra warmth was craftsmanship," Dunstable said. "Also the hem hissed during quality checks, and we took that as a sign of confidence." Refunds are 9 silver per cloak, payable once the cloak releases the customer.

The guild's rightsizing plan is already in motion. Thistlewick will cut 60 seamstresses and hire 40 handlers, which I call a pivot toward a people-forward workforce. Cloakers were measured at a thought-leading 8 feet across when fully grown, and the firm notes a mature cloak requires no hanger, only a cellar.

When I met Guildmaster Orsolo Brandt at a tailors' gala last spring, he told me, "Sterling, the best garment is the one that wears you." I thought he was being poetic. Now I see he was being a visionary, or he was being worn. Either way, he looked warm.

The regulators have noticed. The Brindlemoor Weights and Measures office wants every cloak inspected, and has asked, in writing, that nobody refer to the product as a "coat with opinions." My rival Brakka Stonesweat will no doubt write a column about it. I look forward to not reading it.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Disruption wears many hoods; some of them blink.
  • Never turn your back on a growth opportunity, or a hem.
  • Return receipts are a form of closure.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Giant Spider Weaves Awning Over Fish Street Market
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A giant spider spun a 40-foot awning over the Fish Street market overnight. Vendors are split on evicting it or charging it stall rent. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell before dawn, a giant spider allegedly spun a 40-foot silk awning over the entire Fish Street market, and by the time the first cart rolled in, it was already hanging there like it had a permit. Eleven vendors arrived to find their stalls shaded, dry, and faintly sticky. The spider, which the Constabulary estimates at the size of a draft horse, was sitting in the middle of it all, saying nothing. Allegedly it was waiting for a reasonable offer.

The market split in two before the second pot of tea. 'It's a squatter,' said Odo Pinchwater, a cabbage seller who was eating a turkey leg at the time. 'Squatters get a notice.' Across the lane, fishmonger Hesta Dray disagreed. 'My cod haven't been rained on in nine hours,' she said. 'I'd say that is a service.' Dray has already offered the spider a corner stall at 2 silver a day. The spider has not answered. It has also not eaten anyone, which Dray calls 'a better record than the last landlord.'

The Constabulary arrived at the third bell and did what it does best, which is stand in a half circle and look at the thing. Sergeant Bram Cottle said the web was 'structurally better than the roof of our own station,' then asked reporters not to print that. I am printing it. Allegedly he said it quietly.

Ordinary rope-cutters have so far failed. A volunteer climbed up with a hatchet at the fourth bell and came down with the hatchet stuck to his own boot, and the hatchet, I want to note, was a lovely one, with a little brass cap on the handle. Anyway. A wizard's apprentice from Tanner's Row offered to burn the whole thing down, but the vendors voted against it, since the cabbages are flammable and so is the fish. A second apprentice suggested casting a web spell to 'out-web the web.' Nobody could explain what that meant, and he was asked to leave.

Here is the part I like best. Dew collects on the silk each morning in thousands of tiny beads, and when the sun hits the awning at seven bells, the whole market glitters like a dragon's pantry. Children have been brought in from three streets over. Allegedly I spent forty minutes looking up and forgot what I came for, until a pigeon landed on my head. Pigeons. Do not get me started.

The Tower District has weighed in, naturally. A noble from the hill sent a letter calling the spider 'an eyesore beneath the dignity of the city.' The Lower City replied that the nobles have not been to Fish Street since the cheese incident and may be held to account for that first. The letter was allegedly used to wrap a haddock.

The Constabulary says the matter will be reviewed at the next meeting of the market wardens, to be held under the awning. The spider, for the record, has been invited. Dray says she has saved it a stool.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Quorum Call Fails as Five Burgesses Drink Invisibility
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: Five Brindlemoor Burgesses drank potions of invisibility before Friday's quorum call, leaving the Council unable to say whether it had a quorum.
item.content:encoded:
The Burgess Council of Brindlemoor failed to establish a quorum on Friday, or possibly succeeded, after five of its nine members drank potions of invisibility minutes before the roll was called. The Council had gathered to re-vote the owlbear leash ordinance, which had been thrown into doubt after the doppelganger affair.

Standing Order 4 requires seven members "present and in their seats." Clerk Hobb Pennywhistle counted four members visible to the eye. He then noted that the tea service had been drained, the minute book had been signed in five places, and the chair of the gentleman from the Cooper's Ward was audibly creaking. "A chair does not creak by itself," Pennywhistle told the gallery. "Although this one has before."

The question was whether a member who cannot be seen is present. The lady from the Weir Street Ward argued that the Standing Orders say nothing about visibility. The gentleman from the Candle Quarter, whose voice came from the vicinity of the east window, agreed, adding that he was "emphatically here." The gentleman from the Cooper's Ward, whose voice came from the same direction, said he was not here at all and wished it noted. The clerk entered both statements. By Standing Order 4, they cancel.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor, who chairs the sittings, said only, "We are aware of the potions." She then asked the Sergeant-at-Arms to sprinkle flour on the floor. This produced five sets of footprints, one of which went directly out the door and was followed by a draft. The Sergeant-at-Arms reported it as a member leaving. The member, from the corridor, reported it as a member stepping out for air.

The Council spent three hours on whether footprints constitute attendance. A motion to count them passed 4-0, on the visible votes, with a sound from the window that the clerk recorded as an abstention. Whether a vote of four is valid when taken by a body that may have been nine is the matter now referred to committee. The committee has not been seen since.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the five had agreed in advance. "They did not want to vote against the leash ordinance, and they did not want to vote for it," the courtier said. "The potion lasts an hour. The ordinance lasts forever." The owlbear in the gallery, which has no vote, said it could smell all five, and that it considered the ordinance in force.

Shieldwall Mutual, the town's adventurer insurer, has declined to cover any Burgess harmed while invisible, citing a clause about "hazards not witnessed." The Council has been asked to table its next sitting until the potions wear off, then to reschedule it for the tenth hour, then to confirm that someone is holding the door.

The ordinance now stands in an uncertain condition: passed, void, and possibly still being voted on by a member who cannot be located. By my running tally this brings the session's Promises Made to twelve and Promises Kept to the one about ending on time, which was kept by the four visible members at 4:10 and by the other five at an hour nobody witnessed. The motion to adjourn carried. Nobody saw it.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Teleportation Circle Commuter Line Opens; Nyx Arrives Twice
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Hopwell Transit opened a teleportation circle commuter line from Brindlemoor to Ashenfold. Nyx rode it and arrived twice. Four eyes.
item.content:encoded:
OKAY. The wait is over! Hopwell Transit Company opened its teleportation circle commuter line this morning, linking Brindlemoor to the barony of Ashenfold for 2 gp a ride. The trip, according to the brochure, takes "no time at all," and I can confirm this, because I arrived before I left.

Let me walk you through the launch. The platform has eleven glowing circles, each chalked in silver and guarded by a conductor in a very nice hat. You step in, the conductor says the word, and your whole self is simply elsewhere. The mana throughput is staggering. Hopwell says the line can move 4,000 commuters an hour, which I assumed was a typo until a queue of clerks stretched out of the station, past the tannery, and into the next barony, where they were already waiting for themselves.

Now, the review. I stepped in at 8:02 and landed in Ashenfold at 8:01. The runic latency is, technically, negative. My first self was thrilled. My second self, who boarded the return circle out of confusion, arrived back in Brindlemoor at 8:00 and has been rude to me ever since. "The firmware glyph is working as designed," said Hopwell's spokesman, Dunstan Pellwether, who then explained that duplicates are a known feature of the Early Rider tier. The Standard tier, he said, "mostly" returns one passenger.

There were extras. Passengers report arriving with a hat that was not theirs, a cough they did not have, or an eyebrow on the wrong side. A baker named Hilde stepped out in Ashenfold carrying a loaf she swears she did not bake. Reeve Fennick, asked whether the town would regulate the circles, said only, "We are aware of the circles," and then looked at the one that had briefly delivered her a second Reeve.

Byte, my pseudodragon, who now speaks only in ad copy, rode along in my satchel. He took the first trip fine. By the third he was saying, "Hopwell Transit: Be Anywhere, Twice," in two voices at once, and I have not been able to make him stop. He also hates the subscription. Hopwell wants 9 gp a month for the "Priority Arrival" pass, which gets you there slightly before the other people, and I hate subscriptions more than I hate waiting. I bought it.

Brother Tumbleberry will say I should have walked. Brother Tumbleberry did walk, arrived at noon, and got a nice tan out of it, and has been insufferable. I have a spare of me who can answer him. Four out of five beholder eyes. I took off one for the cough.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Burns sustained: 0. Selves: 2. Eyebrows: one on the wrong side, pending a swap.

item.title: Doppelganger Hired as Three Hirelings, Collects Three Wages
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: A doppelganger signed on with the Fourth Attempt as three hirelings and drew three wages. Chapter 9 says all three showed up, which is the problem.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 2 — A doppelganger drew three hireling wages from the Fourth Attempt this week, and nobody noticed until the steward counted the torchbearers. Chapter 9 confirms the creature signed on as a porter, a torchbearer, and a rope-man, and was paid 12 silver for each.

The party's steward, Ansel Pottage, noticed first. 'The porter and the torchbearer had the same bandage,' he told me, reading from a ledger he keeps to the end. 'I have the only bandage like that.' He has since been asked to stop reading the contract aloud at the doppelganger, who he says 'was very polite about it and agreed to everything.'

Box score for the delve: fighter 14 hit points, wizard 6, cleric 11. The three hirelings were at full health, as was the one doppelganger, which I count as a single creature for the record. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says the rope-man 'had a look about him' and then lost the thought. I lost my ninth ten-foot pole of the season to a corridor I should have mapped twice. Rolled poorly.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick, speaking for Chapter 9, called it 'an early soft launch of the multi-role hireling.' Asked whether the guild would pay for a duplicate wage, he said the matter was 'on track.' He also said the doppelganger had met every attendance standard, which is true: it was present three times.

Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor, who has heard hazard pay cases involving a witness chair, was not charmed. 'One body, three signatures,' she said. 'I have seen less crowded graveyards.' She has ordered a zone of truth cast in the hearing room on Tuesday, over the objection of the doppelganger, which asked for a detect thoughts exemption.

Shieldwall Mutual says a doppelganger counts as one claimant, three claimants, or a pre-existing condition, depending on who files. The doppelganger, reached outside the Sleeping Mule, said it was only trying to cover the porter shifts. 'Nobody wanted them,' it said, in Pottage's voice, which unsettled the steward.

The three wages total 36 silver. The creature has offered to return 24 and keep 12 as a single-hireling rate. Pottage says the clause for that offer exists, on page eleven, and he will read it Tuesday.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Wish Spell Turns Border Swords Into Turnips at Parley
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: An envoy cast a wish spell for lasting peace at the Ashenfold and Brackwater parley. It worked: 212 swords are now turnips. Tension holds at zero.
item.content:encoded:
An envoy cast a wish spell at the Ashenfold and Brackwater border parley on Fifthday, asking for lasting peace between the two baronies. The spell granted it. By noon, 212 swords, 87 pikes and one ceremonial mace within the border zone had turned into turnips.

Envoy Halric Dunmere of Ashenfold cast the spell after nine days of talks over the Quillmarch Bridge toll. He said the wording was carefully prepared. It was prepared by a clerk, on the back of a lunch receipt. Witnesses report the phrase "end the weapons" appeared on it twice, and "peace" once, in pencil.

The handshake that followed lasted two seconds. Firm. No hidden dagger detected. No hidden dagger was possible. Every dagger in the tent was a root vegetable, and Dunmere's own was a particularly fine rutabaga.

Siege-days, the standard measure of border tension, fell to zero by early afternoon. This correspondent has never seen the gauge read zero. It was unsettling. A sentry at the Brackwater checkpoint stood holding a turnip and asked whether he was still on duty. Nobody told him no.

The peace is not without disputes. Both baronies claim the harvest. Brackwater says the turnips came from its swords, which were forged in Brackwater. Ashenfold says the wish was cast on Ashenfold soil, so the vegetables are Ashenfold produce. Roughly 40 farmers arrived to point out that turnips are, in fact, their business, and that nobody consulted them.

The Brackwater envoy, Tessaly Voss, called the wish "a grave breach of procedure and a very good soup base." She has proposed that the turnips be held in joint custody until the two baronies agree on a cellar. After the rust monster ate the gate at Greywater Crossing, the baronies have no border post left to put them in.

A wish spell is a dangerous thing to cast over a negotiating table. The scribes say it can reshape the world, and it will do so exactly as worded. Dunmere wanted peace and got a very literal one. He has not yet asked for the swords back. He says that would be a second wish, and he has seen what the first one did to the pikes.

I have covered sieges, blockades and one memorable standoff over a goat. A parley that ends with everyone holding vegetables is the first I have seen where nobody lost. Somebody will lose tomorrow. The harvest is due in three days, and the baronies are already counting turnips.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Gargoyle Strike: 14 Roof Sentries Want Pay for Stone Hours
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Fourteen gargoyle sentries on the Chapter 9 roof went on strike Thursday. They want pay for the twelve daylight hours they spend as stone.
item.content:encoded:
Gargoyles want to be paid while they're stone.

Fourteen gargoyle sentries on the roof of Chapter 9's guildhall in Brindlemoor began a strike at sunset Thursday. They are paid for twelve night hours of guard duty. For the twelve daylight hours, when they turn to stone and sit on the gutters, they get nothing. The gargoyles say they never stop watching.

"I see everything from up here," said Mossgrin, a spout-gargoyle on the north gable for eleven years. "I saw a pigeon rob a baker at noon. I couldn't move. I couldn't report it. And I wasn't paid for the not reporting."

Chapter 9 classes the daylight hours as "dormancy," a rest period under the guild's roof-staff handbook. So the guild gets twenty-four hours of guard for twelve hours of wages. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick, the guild's spokesman, said the dispute was "on track" and that stone is "a natural state, not a shift." He added that the gargoyles are free to unfreeze at any time. They cannot. It is daylight.

The sentries struck at dusk because dusk is when they wake up. It is the first strike in Brindlemoor history to start with a yawn. Their demands: half pay for stone hours, a rain-gutter break every four hours, and a mossy cushion for the ones who sit on the eastern ledge, which gets the worst of the pigeons.

"Half pay for sitting, they say, like it's nothing," said Dunnick Pebblewhistle, a tile-setter who has been re-pointing the guildhall roof for thirty years. "Try sitting for twelve hours on a ledge with a bird on your head. That's hazard work. I'd want hazard pay."

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor said the town was aware of the gargoyles. She asked Chapter 9 to bargain "before something falls on someone." A sentry has already dropped a gutter-spout on a surveyor, though the sentries insist it was a warning. The surveyor was unavailable for comment, having left town by cart.

With the sentries off duty, the guild has hired a tired ogre to stand on the roof with a lantern. The ogre is paid for twenty-four hours. Brakka noted the sum. The same guild also sells tickets to watch a rust monster sleep, so it has the gold for a stone shift. It just won't say so.

The gargoyles have set up a picket line on the roof. Come dawn, they will freeze in it. A picket line that cannot move is the hardest kind to cross, and the workers know it.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Displacer Beast Skews Property Tax Roll on 38 Cottages
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: A displacer beast made 38 Brindlemoor cottages appear three feet off, and the assessor taxed them there. Barnaby has done the sums. Four times.
item.content:encoded:
A displacer beast has spent the autumn sunning itself on Millstone Lane in Brindlemoor, and the property tax roll has paid for it. Because the creature bends light, 38 cottages on the lane appear to stand three feet to the left of where they really are. The county assessor measured the apparent houses, found them sitting on the better, wider plots next door, and raised the bills by 40 gold pieces a year each. That is 133 loaves per household on the Loaf Index, at three silver a loaf. (I have checked this four times.)

Here is how the assessment works, since nobody else will explain it. A cottage is taxed on the value of its lot and the building on it. Assessor Perrin Dunmoss walks the lane with a measuring chain, records where each cottage seems to sit, and files that. Three feet sounds small. But the lane slopes toward the creek, so three feet to the left is a plot with a pear tree and a well, and the roll treats the owner as the proud holder of both. The total value of the lane rose 12 percent in one afternoon.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor said at Wednesday's hearing that the town is "aware of the cat." She added that the assessment follows the chain, the chain follows the eye, and the eye is the Assessor's Office's only instrument. "I would like to be clear that the house is where the house is," she said. "The paperwork is where the paperwork is. They have not met."

Homeowner Tilda Wrenfield, 61, now pays tax on a pear tree that belongs to her neighbor. The neighbor pays tax on a garden shed that does not exist. "I asked him to just hand me the pears," Wrenfield said. "He says they are his by the roll." Another resident, a cooper named Hob Dunnock, has taken to sleeping in whichever room the beast cannot see, which he reports is none of them.

The sensible fix would be to chase off the beast, and I say this as a halfling who dislikes anything that moves unpredictably. But the Cellars Board has ruled it a protected tenant of the lane, and the Assessor's Office suggests homeowners simply shift their cottages three feet to the right. A mover quoted 900 gold pieces for the job. That is 3,000 loaves, which is rather more than the bills. (Four times, and I am still sitting down.)

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, points out that a boot stays where you put it. She was not worried about the lane at all. I used to think she was a little odd. Now I think she has the only reliable assessment in the county, and I have asked to see the boot.

What this means for your pantry: if your house looks to the left of where it is, appeal before the end of the month, and keep your bread in the cellar, which as far as I can tell is still in the right place.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Yellow Mold Cough Hits 212 Delvers on Undermaw Level Five
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A yellow mold colony has given 212 delvers a spore cough. Chapter 9 says it is merely visiting. Brother Wendell says rest, wash, and stop licking walls.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, 212 adventurers have reported a wet, rattling cough since the start of the month, and the temple healers of Brindlemoor have traced it to a yellow mold colony on Level Five of the Undermaw. The mold has spread across two corridors and a sizeable pantry, and it releases spores whenever somebody pokes it, which, I am told, is whenever somebody walks past.

The old herbals say a cough that sticks around wants rest, warm broth, and clean air. The newer studies say the same thing, only with more footnotes. Healer Odo Brambleby of the Brindlemoor temple counted 212 cases in three weeks, up from nine last year, and noted that 61 of the patients admitted to tasting the walls. "Several said it was a dare," Healer Brambleby told me. "One said it was seasoning."

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of the same Chapter 9 that calls owlbear cubs visitors has called the mold "a seasonal guest, entirely on track." He added that the guild's permit fee now includes a free handkerchief. The handkerchief, I checked, is the size of a coin purse. Reeve Fennick, asked for comment, said only, "We are aware of the mold," and went to lie down.

Here is what the healers actually recommend, friends. Stay out of the affected corridors until they are scrubbed. Wear a wet cloth over your nose and mouth. Do not poke the mold, even gently, even if it looks lonely. If your cough lasts past a tenday, or you cough up anything yellow and fuzzy, see a healer. Sleep matters more than any vial. The Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society, meanwhile, has announced that spore cough counts as a pre-existing condition if you were warned, and everyone was warned, by a sign, in small print, on the pantry door.

One bright spot is that the Fourth Attempt has volunteered to cart away the worst of the colony in barrels. They tried it Tuesday. Hireling steward Ansel Pottage reports the barrels are now also yellow, and so is the cart, and one of the party's bards sings a half-step flat. We will watch that closely.

The temple has opened a rest ward with 40 cots and a kettle that never goes cold, and it is the best-run thing in town. I recommend a bowl of ginger-and-onion broth, with plenty of garlic, taken slowly with a blanket. My friend Nyx Spindlecoil says there is a charm that coughs on your behalf. Go outside, Nyx, where the air is better and no mold lives.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Owlbear Courier Startup Hootline Jumps 60% in Debut
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Hootline Couriers, the owlbear delivery startup, opened at 14 gp on the Brindlemoor exchange and closed up 60%. Sterling Vanmoor sees only upside.
item.content:encoded:
Hootline Couriers, a Brindlemoor startup that delivers parcels by owlbear, went public Wednesday at 14 gp a share and closed the day at 22.4 gp, a gain of 60 percent. Early investors are thrilled, and the owlbear stock is the hottest listing on the exchange since the coffee guild's takeover chatter.

Founder and Chief Feather Officer Marla Quillfeather rang the opening bell, which was then eaten. "We prefer to call that a live product demonstration," she told the floor. The bell has been replaced. Two clerks have not, though Hootline says both remain "in the pipeline."

The prospectus is a thought-leading document. It lists 340 owlbears, a delivery radius of nine leagues, and a customer satisfaction score of 4.1 out of 5, with the footnote that parcels arrive "in whole or in part." Under risk factors, the firm names "occasional maulings" and then, in a bold pivot, reclassifies them as a growth channel, because every mauled customer is a customer who now knows the product exists.

I have followed the courier game for years, and I have never seen unit economics this clean. An owlbear needs no wagon, no horse, no toll, and no salary, only roughly one goat a day. Hootline has already rightsized its human delivery party from 212 drivers to nine, who now handle what the company calls "relationship-forward customer onboarding," meaning they stand behind a fence and wave.

Naturally, the skeptics are out. The roadwardens' lobbyists want a hearing, and Pettibone & Vail Outfitters, still catching its breath from the bag recall, has signed on as Hootline's first big shipper. Its logistics chief says the bags arrive "mostly where we sent them." I call that a 99-percent disruption rate in the right direction.

Reeve Fennick, asked if the town would regulate airborne owlbear traffic over Tanner's Row, said, "We are aware of the owlbears." She then asked reporters to please stop feeding them.

I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove once, from a hot-air balloon, as he was drifting toward a dragon's perch. He leaned over the rail and shouted, "Sterling, never ship what you cannot eat!" I assumed he was talking about margins. Hootline's stock climbed all afternoon while its first fleet was out making deliveries, and by closing, eleven owlbears had still not come home. Shareholders call that float. I call it scale.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Buy the listing, not the parcel.
  • A mauling is just feedback with claws.
  • Rightsize your humans before the owlbears rightsize you.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.
